analysis.one_liner: Bars states from stopping women from traveling out of state for abortion care.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by all 186 House Democrats who cosponsored it, never got a committee hearing or a floor vote and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, several states banned abortion and some threatened penalties for residents who traveled elsewhere for care. This bill would have made it illegal under federal law for anyone enforcing state rules to block, restrict, or retaliate against a person who crosses state lines for a legal abortion, a provider serving out-of-state patients, or anyone helping them travel. It also protected the interstate movement of FDA-approved abortion pills, and let the Justice Department and private citizens sue violators.
analysis.who_benefits: Women living in states with abortion bans, especially those with lower incomes who lack the means to overcome legal threats or travel obstacles, plus the clinics, providers, and helpers (funds, employers) who would otherwise face lawsuits or prosecution for assisting them.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits anyone acting under state law from preventing, restricting, impeding, or retaliating against a person who travels across state lines for an abortion, anyone who helps them travel, providers serving out-of-state patients, and anyone helping those providers. [S2][S3]
Prohibits interference with the movement of FDA-approved abortion drugs across state lines, protecting access to medication abortion by mail. [S2][S3]
Enforced by the Attorney General via civil actions and through a private right of action with damages, attorney's fees, and costs, giving patients and providers a legal remedy. [S2][S3]

analysis.who_pays: State officials and private bounty-style enforcers of abortion bans in restrictive states would lose the ability to police patients who leave the state, and anti-abortion advocacy groups that support travel restrictions would lose a policy goal.

drawbacks.text: Opponents argue the bill reaches beyond the federal government's recognized power over interstate travel and commerce, intruding on state authority to regulate medicine within their borders. [S3]

The bill protects the right to travel for abortion but does not require any state to provide or pay for abortion care, and its protection of FDA-approved drugs could face federal courts skeptical of codifying medication abortion distribution rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a targeted federal protection that would have secured access to legal abortion for people in states with bans, at a cost to states and groups seeking to restrict that access. Its limits: it did not restore abortion care in-state or resolve broader legal and political uncertainty, and would likely have faced court challenges.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in committee without a hearing or a vote until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025. [S1][S5]

narrative.text: Introduced on February 2, 2023 by Rep. Lizzie Fletcher (D-TX) and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce. [S1][S2]
Referred to the Subcommittee on Health on February 10, 2023, and never advanced further. [S1][S5]
Died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025. [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State governments with abortion bans and opponents of abortion access benefited from the bill dying, as did the status quo of no federal protection for interstate abortion travel.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States and groups opposing abortion access

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a hearing or markup; referred it to the Subcommittee on Health where it stalled.

against.name: House Majority Leadership
against.what_they_did: Controlled floor scheduling and committee agendas in the 118th Congress; never brought the bill to a vote.

against.name: Abortion-rights opponents / anti-abortion advocacy groups
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed federal legislation to protect interstate abortion access.

sides.party_line_note: 186 of 216 House Democrats cosponsored the bill, while no Republicans did and the Republican-led committee never acted on it.
